newsitem.title: USA: Tough times still ahead for refiners - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Tough times still ahead for refiners - analyst.

text.p: U.S. oil refiners, faced with poor profits and the prospect of consolidation, can expect more hard times in the coming years, an analyst told refining executives at an industry conference here Monday.

"As the U.S. refining industry moves into the 21st century, the underlying fundamentals will likely remain weak," Thomas Kellagher, a consultant with Houston-based McKinsey & Co Inc told executives at the National Petroleum Refiners Association (NPRA) annual meeting.
He noted that while thirst for refined products will likely grow in coming years, so too will refining capacity--in part because of what he called an overly fragmented industry.
"Despite a signficant number of transactions, industry consolidation has not happened," Kellagher said.

"A very favorable future scenario would have a much more concentrated industry structure with a persistent surplus of heavy crude oil," he said, noting industry ownership is now more fragmented than it was just over 10 years ago.
He said the 10 largest companies now account for only 54 percent of capacity, compared to 61 percent in 1986.
Regarding heavy crude supplies, he noted that they will likely arrive from producers like Venezuela or Mexico, but those will be accompanied in time by new refining capacity.

"Additional supplies of heavy crude oil could lead to improvement of deep resid conversion economics," he said referring to processing cheap heavy crudes into residual fuel, which is in turn refined into valuable products like gasoline.
"But this is likely to be a temporary improvement due to the strong incentives for producing countries to ensure adequate upgrading capacity to maximize the value of heavy crude," Kellagher said.
He also said the profit advantages some players now enjoy in certain niches, such as the West Coast are likely to erode as distribution logistics from distant refiner centers improve.

"Declining domestic crude oil production in Alaska and California will result in higher crude prices and lower profit margins for West Coast refiners as more costly imported crude oils fill the gap," he said.

He said midcontinent and Rocky Mountain refiners may suffer a similar fate as local production falls in the Rocky Mountain region and Canadian crudes flow into Chicago-area markets on more efficient and extensive pipelines.
Additionally, he noted Gulf Coast refiners will likely continue to suffer from intense competition.
"On balance this scenario would not be much different than the last 10 years in terms of average industry financial performance," Kellagher said.
But he stressed that those companies which focus intently on the challenges that lie ahead are likely to rise to the top of the heap and survive.

"While the industry conditions will likely remain challenging, companies that aspire to excel will find ways to leverage all ... sources of competitive advantage -- cost efficiency, asset management and location advantages."
